The data tells a pretty clear story: ICE is strategically targeting specific regions, and most people arrested have no criminal history. More analysis, including downloadable maps, graphs, and summary data, on my Substack:

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…
Interesting methodological finding: criminal history classifications do shift between initial arrest and data export but only in about 0.23–3.29% of cases depending on time elapsed.

New field office data lets us drill below the state level. The St. Paul ICE office alone accounts for a massive share of Minnesota's January 2026 surge. This geographic precision is a major analytical leap forward for tracking enforcement.

West Virginia hasn't gotten much media attention, but it should. ICE arrests there climbed sharply from October 2025 through January 2026, with "other immigration violators" (people with no criminal history) making up the vast majority.

Illinois tells a similar story. ICE arrests surged in October 2025 (driven largely but not exclusively  by people with no criminal record) then collapsed. The data confirms what reporting on Chicago enforcement showed, this was a targeted, time-limited surge.
Minnesota saw a huge spike in ICE arrests in January 2026, largest group was people with no criminal history. This corresponds directly to Operation Metro Surge targeting the Twin Cities metro area.

Despite "public safety" justifications for mass deportation, ICE's monthly arrest totals have not grown since spring 2025. In fact, arrests of people with no criminal history peaked in late 2025 and have since declined. (Non-cit. commit crimes at lower rates than USCs.)

Deportation Data Project just released new data. I shared the validation results, field updates, and initial findings the other day. Now here's some data viz from that post re: the ICE arrest data. What do you see? 🧵

I dig into all of this (the data, the geography, the legal architecture) in my latest Substack post. If this kind of analysis is useful to you, consider subscribing. 
austinkocher.substack.com/p/trumps-deportation-machine-is-getting

None of this means deportations have stopped. People are still being arrested, detained, and deported. Families are still being separated. The harm is real and ongoing. But the gap between rhetoric and operational capacity is widening, not closing.

Trump attended oral arguments (apparently a first for a sitting president) but left after 81 minutes, departing 5 minutes into the opposing side's argument. It captured the administration's posture in miniature.

Only Justices Alito and Thomas appeared open to the government's position. Justice Kavanaugh suggested the Court could resolve the case simply by reaffirming Wong Kim Ark. ACLU attorney Cecillia Wang replied with one word: "Yes." The courtroom laughed.

The 14th Amendment has guaranteed birthright citizenship for 125+ years, reaffirmed in U.S. v. Wong Kim Ark (1898). The government's argument relied on what Chief Justice Roberts called "quirky" and "idiosyncratic" reasoning.
